video_title: The $1/Hour Robot Is Coming: Four Industry Leaders Explain What’s Next
gist: Four back-to-back interviews from the Machina conference in Paris (Peter Funkhouser of Anyotics, Bert Borick of 1X, Amanda McMaster of Boston Dynamics, Jonathan Hurst of Agility Robotics) lay out the commercial state of legged and humanoid robotics: quadruped inspection is already a profitable industrial business priced against downtime, not labor, while humanoids are converging on a labor-priced ~$1/hour cost curve that only arrives after ~100,000-unit scale. The operators agree perception is essentially solved and that the binding constraint is now robot-control data and reliability, and they split sharply on China exposure, weaponization, and how soon 'hard takeoff' arrives (Borick's personal bet: 3 years).

insights.claim: Anyotics sells quadruped inspection robots in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars per unit and justifies that price because the industrial assets they monitor lose revenue in the hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour when they go down, so a single avoided outage pays for the robot.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: The buying trigger for industrial robotics is downtime avoidance, not wage arbitrage — model TAM off asset-uptime budgets rather than headcount.
insights.quote: These assets, if they stop, they lose revenues in hundreds of thousands per hour.

insights.claim: Anyotics explicitly does not sell labor replacement; its pitch is superhuman sensing — thermal cameras, acoustic microphones and gas-concentration sensors that detect micro gas leaks and equipment overheating that human eyes and ears cannot perceive.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: The sensor payload, not the legs, is where margin and defensibility sit in industrial quadrupeds.
insights.quote: For us, it's not about labor replacement, right?

insights.claim: Robotic inspection raises inspection frequency by roughly an order of magnitude — customers who manually inspected once or twice a day now run eight to twenty missions a day, with some running missions up to 40 times a day to catch specific events such as an electric arc furnace firing.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Value comes from data cadence, not cost per inspection — a fleet metric investors can underwrite against downtime savings.

insights.claim: Demand for robot endurance tops out around eight hours of runtime because inspection has diminishing returns to frequency; Anyotics robots run roughly two-hour missions with automated docking-station charging and no battery hot-swap.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Battery energy density is not the binding constraint in industrial inspection — a caution against overweighting battery-breakthrough narratives in this segment.
insights.quote: So the maximum is in the I 8 hour range.

insights.claim: Compute in industrial robots is permanently split: obstacle avoidance and data-quality checks must run on-robot in real time because connectivity cannot be guaranteed and a blurry image uploaded to the cloud is already too late, while contextual and historic downtime analysis runs in the cloud.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Sustained demand for expensive on-robot GPUs — edge silicon content per robot does not collapse as cloud models improve.

insights.claim: The highest-value robotic inspection deployments are offshore oil rigs and offshore wind transformer stations, where each crew helicopter flight costs tens of thousands of dollars.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Offshore energy operators are the highest-willingness-to-pay early adopters; watch for robotics line items in offshore opex budgets.
insights.quote: Every helicopter flight costs in the tens of thousands.

insights.claim: Anyotics has built a robot certified not to create a spark so it can operate in explosive atmospheres such as methane-laden oil, gas and chemical sites — a regulatory-grade capability rather than a demo feature.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Safety certification is a slow-to-copy moat that cheap hardware entrants cannot short-circuit.
insights.quote: we built a special robot that's guaranteed not to create a spark.

insights.claim: Physical intervention — actually fixing the leak the robot detects — is not commercially available: closing levers and opening cabinets are the first steps, and reaching 99.9% reliability for manipulation in explosive atmospheres is still in development despite working demos.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Detect-only is the shipping product; any valuation assuming near-term robotic repair revenue is pricing a capability that vendors say is years out.
insights.quote: getting to 99.9% reliability in explosive atmosphere that's still in development

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot has over 500 customers across 46 countries and is, by the company's claim, the most-used mobile autonomous robot on the planet, doing daytime industrial inspection (acoustic, gauge reading, vibration detection) and nighttime security perimeter work.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: A concrete installed-base benchmark for the leading quadruped, and the reference point competitors' unit counts should be judged against.
insights.quote: we have over 500 customers over 46 countries

insights.claim: Spot is sold capex at roughly $100,000 for a base robot up to $300,000 in the first year fully loaded with services, integration and deployment, while Boston Dynamics expects to use a robot-as-a-service model for the Atlas humanoid because buyers will want to flex capacity up and down.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Quadrupeds monetize as capital equipment; humanoids are being positioned as recurring-revenue services — a materially different revenue-quality profile between the two product lines.
insights.quote: It's the price of a Tesla to a Ferrari depending on how you equip it.

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics measures reliability as mean time between intervention and is now above 3,000 hours, meaning a human touches the robot only a couple of times a year, with a roughly 90-minute battery and self-docking charging so a second robot covers the gap.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Mean time between intervention is the operational KPI that determines whether robot fleets are actually cheaper than labor — use it to compare vendors.
insights.quote: we're um at over 3,000 hours. So only only a couple times a year does a human have to be involved

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics sells on avoided-loss outcomes rather than headcount reduction, citing a customer air leak the robot found that would otherwise have cost $3 million a day, and says industrial customers need to see ROI in under two years.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: A sub-two-year payback hurdle is the gating metric for industrial robot adoption — it defines the maximum price any vendor can charge.
insights.quote: customers need to see your ROI in under two years.

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics argues many inspection tasks were not actually being performed by humans even when assigned, so its deployments create new inspection coverage rather than displacing existing labor.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: If true, early robotics revenue is incremental spend rather than a labor-budget transfer, which changes both TAM sizing and the political risk profile.

themes.theme: China exposure and robot data sovereignty

insights.claim: Anyotics sources zero percent of its robot from China, a position that arose historically from local sourcing and US chips but has become a selling point for customers in critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: China-free bills of materials are becoming a procurement requirement in energy and critical infrastructure — a pricing premium and a supply-chain cost drag simultaneously.

insights.claim: Anyotics argues Chinese robots are excellent hardware that does not solve the customer problem, because buyers compare full solutions — autonomy, inspection intelligence, workflow integration and ISO cybersecurity certification — not walking platforms.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: If the moat is software and integration, cheap Chinese hardware compresses the hardware line but need not compress solution pricing — test this by watching Western win rates in industrial RFPs.
insights.quote: that device is a piece of hardware that can walk beautifully. Great engineering. Love it. Do back flips.

insights.claim: The security objection to foreign robots is framed as camera and data control rather than autonomy risk: an inspection robot is fifteen cameras roaming inside critical infrastructure under someone else's control.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Expect robotics to be regulated on the Huawei/TikTok data-security template, not on safety grounds — the faster path to import restrictions.
insights.quote: you don't want to have 15 cameras in your critical infrastructure that somebody else controls.

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics builds 100% of its robots outside China and Taiwan, and its interim CEO says humanoid robots from China should not be allowed into the United States under any circumstances, citing leaks from Chinese quadrupeds already deployed in the US being back-channelled to China.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: A sitting US robotics CEO publicly lobbying for an import ban is an early signal of policy risk for China-linked robot suppliers and their US channel partners.
insights.quote: It's not safe.

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics frames robotics as a repeat of the semiconductor loss to China and is pushing for a national robotics strategy covering IP protection and onshoring or allied-shoring of the manufacturing ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Positions robotics as a candidate for CHIPS-Act-style subsidies and export controls — a policy catalyst worth tracking for US and allied robotics suppliers.
insights.quote: we have seen what happens if we let China win in the semiconductor space. You know, we can't do that with robotics.

insights.claim: The strategic objective stated by Boston Dynamics is platform standard-setting, not just domestic wins — ensuring the rest of the world adopts the American robotics platform rather than China's.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Frames robotics as a platform land-grab where installed base and ecosystem lock-in matter more than near-term unit margin.
insights.quote: not only do we have to win this, we have to make sure that the rest of the world uses our platform rather than China's.

insights.claim: Core robot component expertise — actuators and similar parts — is concentrated in only three regions, China first plus Europe and the US, while pure labor assembly can be sourced anywhere.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Actuator suppliers in Europe and the US are the chokepoint beneficiaries of any China-decoupling in robotics.

insights.claim: Anyotics refuses military work not on philosophy alone but on product logic: military autonomy requires millisecond human-in-the-loop remote control and different communications, whereas industrial inspection autonomy assumes setup time and unattended operation, so it would require a separate team and product.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that industrial robot makers can pivot into the defense budget cheaply — defense robotics is a separate build, favoring dedicated defense-tech entrants.

insights.claim: Four years ago Anyotics co-signed a letter with Boston Dynamics and other robot makers condemning the weaponization of robots, and its CEO says the technology is not mature enough to responsibly put a gun on it.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: An industry-wide voluntary restraint pact is the thing that breaks first under geopolitical pressure — its collapse would be the signal that armed ground robots are a real market.
insights.quote: we wrote a letter together with our friends at Boston Dynamics and others right who condemn the weaponization of robots

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics maintains an anti-weaponization stance but its interim CEO frames it as business focus rather than philosophy, and says the company already does non-weaponization government work today including explosive ordnance disposal.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: A focus-based rather than principle-based stance is reversible — Boston Dynamics defense revenue is a live option, not a closed door.
insights.quote: we have an anti-weaponization stance

insights.claim: Pressed on whether Boston Dynamics would build armed robots if China fields them, its interim CEO declined to rule it out, saying the company would make the right decision when the time comes while insisting it does not have to decide today.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Read as a soft option on defense revenue for Hyundai-owned Boston Dynamics if Chinese armed ground robots are deployed.

insights.claim: Armed quadruped demonstrations coming out of China are, in the view of a European quadruped CEO, still early tests and demonstrations rather than mature deployed capability, unlike drones in Ukraine which matured out of battlefield necessity.
insights.speaker: Peter Funkhouser, Anyotics co-founder and CEO
insights.so_what: Tempers the armed-robot threat narrative — the near-term defense robotics money is still in drones, not legged platforms.

insights.claim: 1X commits to shipping the Neo home humanoid in 2026 but only to a handful of customers, with an explicitly slow ramp and an admission the product will be rough around the edges and the robots will fall.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: The 2026 'home humanoid' milestone is a vanguard shipment, not a volume market — discount revenue models that assume meaningful 2026 consumer units.
insights.quote: Getting a home humanoid in 2026 is going to be rough around the edges

insights.claim: 1X sold out its first 10,000 Neo pre-orders in the first few days under two models — an early-adopter upfront full payment and a roughly $500-per-month subscription — and the subscription structure is still evolving alongside the product.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: Demonstrated consumer willingness to pay a car-payment-sized monthly fee for an unproven humanoid — a demand datapoint for the whole consumer robotics category.
insights.quote: we sold out the first 10K in uh the first few days

insights.claim: 1X is turning Neo into an open platform — a consumer skill/app store plus a developer stack with fleet management, tactile-sensor data-collection gloves and in-house fine-tuning — and will allow third parties, including rival foundation labs, to run their own models on Neo hardware.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: A humanoid vendor deliberately commoditizing its own model layer to win the hardware standard — the iPhone/Android question for humanoids is being decided now.

insights.claim: Teleoperation is a permanent product feature rather than a temporary crutch, because remote physical presence — the CEO's example of running his company through a Neo while travelling, plus unmanned remote power stations where a technician is an hour's drive away — has no autonomy substitute for rare one-off events.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: Telepresence robotics is a distinct revenue line with its own economics; humanoid business cases should not be judged solely on autonomy percentage.
insights.quote: Put the hat on Neo. I am Neo.

insights.claim: Neo's hardware has outrun teleoperation: the new hands are more capable than a remote operator can exploit because the operator does not feel what the robot feels, and building full haptic systems would make the interface slow and clunky.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual bottleneck story — the constraint is the human interface, which pushes 1X toward sensor-wearing data collection and away from haptic-suit vendors.
insights.quote: The teleoperator will not feel the same as the robot is feeling for example.

insights.claim: A significant share of current demand on 1X's platform comes from customers wanting to automate laboratory work, on the logic that an AI model cannot advance science unless it can physically build and run experiments and observe results.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: Lab automation is an early, non-obvious revenue beachhead for general-purpose humanoids — relevant to pharma and CRO capex.
insights.quote: a lot of the demand that we're seeing now on our platform is people who want to automate lab work

themes.theme: The data pyramid and 1X's internet-video bet

insights.claim: 1X organizes robot training data as a pyramid: a small high-quality teleoperation set used only to align the model, a larger set gathered by humans wearing the robot's sensors and gloves, egocentric human video, and at the base a ludicrously immense pool of general internet video.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: A concrete taxonomy for evaluating any robotics company's data strategy — ask which layer they can actually access at scale.

insights.claim: 1X's decade-long structural bet is that making the robot mechanically similar enough to a human lets it train on all available human video, and the company claims it now has scaling laws showing this works, which is why it started its world model lab.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: If human-video pre-training scales, anthropomorphic robots gain a data advantage that non-humanoid form factors structurally cannot match.
insights.quote: if you get the robot to be similar enough to a human then you can train on all of the available video data out there of humans

insights.claim: 1X argues achieving true robotic intelligence requires multiple orders of magnitude more data than anyone can collect via egocentric or sensor data in the next few years, making general internet video the only viable path and creating a catch-22 for competitors relying on collected data.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: A direct bear case on robotics startups whose primary asset is a proprietary teleop or wearable dataset.
insights.quote: you need multiple orders of magnitude more data than anyone is even close to collecting over the next few years with egocentric data or with this sensor data

insights.claim: 1X's CEO says he is extremely sure hard takeoff — robots building robots, data centers, chip fabs and doing mining and refining in a self-sufficient system — is less than a decade away, with a personal bet of three years.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: The most aggressive timeline stated by any of the four operators; if even directionally right it reprices industrial labor, mining and construction — and it is falsifiable within three years.
insights.quote: I am extremely sure that we're less than a decade away from hard takeoff.

insights.claim: 1X argues AGI cannot be reached without robotics because digital intelligence can never create its own physical substrate, making embodiment a prerequisite rather than an application of AI.
insights.speaker: Bert Borick, founder and CEO of 1X
insights.so_what: If accepted, robotics becomes a required capex leg of the AGI trade rather than an adjacent sector.
insights.quote: the digital intelligence can never create its own substrate you need the physical part

themes.theme: Humanoid unit economics versus human labor

insights.claim: Agility Robotics expects Digit V5 to run about 20 out of 24 hours a day thanks to fast charging, which works out to roughly 8,000 hours a year and about 40,000 hours of work over a five-year life.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: The denominator for any humanoid cost-per-hour model — 40,000 lifetime hours is what turns a five-figure robot into a sub-$1/hour cost.

insights.claim: Humanoid robots will only reach a $20,000–$40,000 price point after the industry scales to roughly 100,000 deployed units, which at 40,000 lifetime work hours implies about a dollar an hour against $20–$40 an hour for Western factory labor — roughly 90% cost compression.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, with host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Cumulative unit volume, not model capability, is the gating variable for the $1/hour robot — track industry-wide deployment counts as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: It's going to need to go through the scaling and have 100,000 robots out there before that actually is real.

insights.claim: Agility argues humanoid pricing is anchored to prevailing human wages rather than build cost, so as robots get better and cheaper the price stays inelastic for a long time and the spread accrues to the manufacturer.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Implies expanding gross margins for humanoid makers as BOM falls while pricing tracks wages — the core margin thesis for the sector.
insights.quote: the value for these robots is really set by the human labor and what does it cost to pay people to do these jobs. So it's a very inelastic price for a very long time.

insights.claim: Digit V5, shipping later this year, is claimed to be the first balancing humanoid that can step out of a work cell without a physical barrier separating it from people, which Agility calls its scaling moment.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Barrier-free operation removes the facility retrofit cost that caps humanoid deployment density — the specific product milestone to watch for an inflection in Agility's unit volume.
insights.quote: Digit V5 which is coming out later this year is the first time that a humanoid robot a robot which is balancing can step out of a work cell and does not need a physical barrier between the robot and the person

insights.claim: Agility's Amazon deployment passed all R&D goals but was blocked because it did not meet Amazon's safety requirements, forcing a two-to-three-year bottom-to-top redesign in which every system of the robot was touched to achieve safety.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Safety certification, not capability, is the hidden multi-year gate between a working humanoid demo and enterprise revenue — a timing risk for every new humanoid entrant.

insights.claim: Agility argues humanoids are the wrong form factor for fully lights-out package sortation, where purpose-built specialty automation running 24/7 is more efficient, and that humanoids win specifically in legacy and human-designed spaces such as retail, grocery, hospitals, construction sites and doorstep delivery.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Splits the automation TAM: fixed automation keeps greenfield warehouses while humanoids monetize brownfield and human-facing environments — different competitive sets and margins.
insights.quote: And a humanoid doesn't make sense. It's not the most efficient thing for that specific task. A humanoid is useful for walking into human environments doing human workflows.

insights.claim: Agility demonstrated last-mile delivery roughly seven years ago with Ford — a Digit robot exiting a vehicle, walking up stairs to a front porch and dropping a package — but has deliberately deprioritized it because warehouse work is the bigger first market.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Capability for robotic last-mile delivery has existed for years; the constraint is market prioritization, so a combined robotaxi-plus-humanoid delivery stack could appear faster than expected once economics justify it.

insights.claim: Agility argues the majority of workers in many warehouse and sortation applications are already robots — AMRs, conveyor belts and industrial arms — so humanoids are an incremental new form of automation rather than the start of displacement.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Reframes the humanoid displacement debate — the marginal automation dollar competes against existing fixed automation, not against headcount.

insights.claim: Agility frames robotics as the only route to US GDP growth given a non-growing population and anti-immigration politics, since growth must come from increased efficiency and capability rather than more workers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, with host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The macro argument that gives robotics political cover and potential policy support in the US despite labor-displacement optics.

themes.theme: What is actually solved versus still blocking

insights.claim: Agility's chief robot officer says perception is all but solved and calls it the huge inflection point, because large language models now give robots free semantic understanding of a scene that three or four years ago required narrow hand-programming.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Perception is now commoditized input rather than differentiation — value in robotics is migrating to control, data and safety certification.
insights.quote: the fact that perception is all but solved at this point is a really, really huge inflection point

insights.claim: The binding constraint in robotics is that no internet-scale training set exists for robot control — there is no corpus of torque commands to every motor given all sensor input — so unlike language models the data must be manufactured.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Explains why robotics will not simply ride the LLM curve and why data-generation methods (sim, teleop, video pre-training) are the real competitive axis.
insights.quote: these language models are trained off of the entire data on the internet and that data does not exist for robot control

insights.claim: Agility rejects the idea that world models are a silver bullet, citing a persistent sim-to-real gap from unmodelled physics such as wave dynamics in a liquid and condensation on a glass, which still requires real practice with real robots.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: A direct counterweight to simulation-first robotics narratives — physical fleet hours retain strategic value even in a world-model era.

insights.claim: Agility explicitly rejects a robotics singularity in favor of a snowball model of compounding progress driven by capital, engineering time and parallel exploration of many tools rather than any single breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: The most direct disagreement in the episode with 1X's three-year hard-takeoff call — bracket robotics timelines rather than anchoring to any single operator's forecast.
insights.quote: Think of it more like a snowball picking up steam going down a hill.

insights.claim: Robots remain far worse learners than humans, requiring vastly more data and examples, but they have a structural offsetting advantage: skills learned by one robot transfer over the network to all robots of that type.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics
insights.so_what: Fleet learning turns installed base into a compounding capability moat — favors whoever deploys the most units of a single hardware type first.
insights.quote: Robots take so much more data, so many more examples than a person.

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics splits robot intelligence into two brains — the physical control brain that stays on the robot, and a cloud-capable semantic reasoning layer it may source through partners such as Google DeepMind — with a customer-specific workflow wrapper living in between and placed on-robot or in cloud as needed.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Signals that hardware leaders intend to buy rather than build the reasoning layer, creating an addressable market for foundation-model providers in robotics.

insights.claim: Humanoid battery constraints are being engineered away at the robot level rather than the cell level: Boston Dynamics' Atlas carries two batteries and swaps them itself by rotating its torso, so it never fully powers down, while quadrupeds simply dock and charge.
insights.speaker: Amanda McMaster, interim CEO of Boston Dynamics
insights.so_what: Self-swapping batteries push effective humanoid uptime toward 20+ hours a day, which is what makes the sub-$1/hour cost math work.
